item.title: Why Go: A Language Built for Engineering
item.description:
Why Go?

You might ask: why learn Go? There are so many programming languages—Python is simple and easy to learn, Java has a mature ecosystem, C/C++ delivers unmatched performance, and JavaScript is everywhere. What makes Go special?

Go’s value lies in engineering practice: it aims language design squarely at team collaboration and large-scale software development, not at syntactic expressiveness or theoretical purity.

Go was created in 2007 by a team of engineers at Google with one goal in mind: solve real-world pain points in software development. They wanted fast compilation, simple deployment, easy concurrency handling, and maintainable code. They weren’t looking for the “coolest” language—they wanted the most practical one, where developers can write code quickly, compile fast, run efficiently, and keep things simple and maintainable.

item.title: Basic Syntax: Variables, Types, and Control Flow
item.description:
This article is based on Go 1.26.

In the previous article, we discussed Go’s design philosophy and your first Hello World program. This time, let’s dive directly into syntax—variables, types, control flow, functions, composite types, and pointers. The core goal is simple: enable you to read and write basic Go code.

Go’s syntax design philosophy is simplicity over complexity—eliminating unnecessary syntactic sugar while keeping things clear and intuitive. If you’re coming from another language, you’ll find Go’s learning curve relatively gentle because it has few syntactic features, but each one is practical.

item.title: Interfaces and Generics: Go's Core Abstraction Mechanisms
item.description:
In the previous articles, we covered Go’s basic syntax and concurrency model. Now let’s dive deep into the two core components of Go’s type system—interfaces and generics. These two constitute the foundation of Go’s abstraction mechanisms: interfaces provide runtime polymorphism based on behavior, while generics bring compile-time abstraction with type safety.

Go’s design philosophy always emphasizes simplicity. Interfaces adopt implicit implementation, meaning no explicit declaration of implementation relationships is needed. As long as a type possesses the method set required by an interface, it automatically implements that interface. This duck typing style makes code more natural and reduces unnecessary coupling.

item.title: MiBeeNvr: A Lightweight Home NVR System I Built
item.description:
I have several cameras at home — a few Xiaomi cameras, some DIY ESP32 cameras, and multiple Raspberry Pi CSI cameras. I’d been using cloud storage solutions, but I was never comfortable with them: vendor lock-in, network dependency, and the costs add up. So I decided to build my own NVR system, called MiBeeNvr.

Why Build MiBeeNvr

To be honest, I was never satisfied with existing cloud storage solutions. Take Xiaomi cameras, for example. By default, you can only view them through the Mi Home app. Recordings are either stored on an SD card (limited capacity, frequent plugging/unplugging) or in the cloud. Cloud storage costs tens of dollars per month, and there’s the privacy concern — you never know when the manufacturer might use your video data for AI training or sell it to third parties. Not to mention vendor lock-in — switching platforms is nearly impossible.

item.title: Error Handling: Go's Multi-Return Value Approach
item.description:
Go’s error handling philosophy is “simple, explicit, controllable.” Every function that can fail can return an error value, and the caller must explicitly handle it. No exceptions, no implicit propagation—everything is in plain sight.

The error Interface: One Value, One Method

Go’s error interface is minimal: just one Error() string method.

go
1
2

type error interface {
 Error() string
}

This means any type that implements Error() string is an error. The Go standard library provides many built-in error types, most commonly errors.New and fmt.Errorf.

item.title: Concurrency: The Art of Goroutines, Channels, and Context
item.description:
Concurrency is the core feature that distinguishes Go from other languages. Unlike C++/Java’s thread model, and unlike JavaScript’s single-threaded event loop, Go provides a set of concurrency primitives — goroutines, channels, and context — that let you write high-performance concurrent programs with relatively straightforward code.

This article covers the technical details of Go’s concurrency model: the underlying scheduling mechanism, the implementation of channels and context, common concurrency patterns, and performance optimization and best practices.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.2.0: Live View and Auto-Merging
item.description:
v0.1.0 could only play back recordings — no live view; it shipped binaries only, so Docker users had to roll their own image; recordings landed as 30-second segments, 2,880 files per camera per day; and every camera shared one retention setting, so the front door and the balcony couldn’t be treated differently. v0.2.0 fixes all of that in one go.

Live view, finally

  • Click in the web UI and the live picture plays — nothing to install, H.264 and H.265 both supported
  • Switches to the low-resolution stream automatically when bandwidth is tight
  • Consumes nothing while nobody is watching

Easier to install

  • Two Docker commands and it runs — Raspberry-Pi-class ARM devices included
  • No config file needed on first start; setup happens in the web UI
  • Docker-less Linux machines install with one command and register as a boot-time system service
  • Works on phones too; Chinese/English switchable; light/dark follows the system

Recordings that behave

  • Fragments merge automatically — small segments become large files, faster to manage and search
  • Per-camera retention: keep the front door 30 days, the balcony 7
  • Storage trends and per-camera recording volume visible in the web UI
  • Cheap ESP32-CAM-class cameras connect directly — no protocol conversion to wrestle with

The previous article introduced MiBeeNvr’s basic features and design philosophy. It’s only been a week since v0.1.0, and v0.2.0 follows right behind. This update is substantial — 15 new features, some I needed myself, others from community feedback.

item.title: Standard Library, Testing, and Toolchain: A Panoramic View of Go Engineering Practices
item.description:
After three articles of our journey—why choose Go, basic syntax and concurrency, interfaces and generics—we’ve reached the finale of the Go chapter, time to connect the engineering practices.

Go’s engineering capacity also shows up in its standard library, testing framework, and toolchain. They make up the daily working environment for Go developers and underpin rapid construction of reliable, maintainable software.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.3.1: Multi-Protocol Streaming and Native Xiaomi Camera Support
item.description:
#XQ|A lot of work went into the releases after v0.2.0. v0.3.x brings several major updates: native Xiaomi camera support, recording archiving, multi-protocol streaming architecture (WebRTC/HTTP-FLV/RTMP/SRT/LL-HLS), and a wave of security hardening. The architectural evolution from external dependencies to built-in implementation, from single protocol to full protocol support, was much more complex than I expected.

The previous post introduced v0.2.0’s 15 new features (v0.2.0 Update). If you haven’t read the first post, start with MiBeeNvr Introduction. v0.3.0 focuses on deep Xiaomi camera integration, and v0.3.1 builds on that with a complete multi-protocol streaming architecture. item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.4.0: Audio Recording Pipeline and Multi-Layer Health Monitoring Architecture
item.description:
After v0.3.1 shipped, v0.4.0 is a feature-dense release: audio recording pipeline, multi-layer health monitoring engine, HLS/LL-HLS playback stability optimization, and a major UI redesign. For the full changelog, see GitHub Release Notes.

item.title: Why Rust: A Language Pursuing Zero-Cost Abstractions from a Go Perspective
item.description:
This article is based on Rust 1.82 (released on 2026-01-23, current latest stable version). Rust is a modern systems programming language proven in production. Official documentation is at doc.rust-lang.org, and installation guide is at rust-lang.org/tools/install/.

Why Rust?

If you’ve already mastered Go, you might ask: why learn Rust? Rust exists to fill the performance and control gap that Go leaves open.

Go has conquered cloud-native and microservices domains with its extremely low learning curve, excellent concurrency model, and fast compilation speed. But its garbage collector (GC) and fixed runtime make it constrained in systems programming, embedded, and high-performance scenarios. When you need more precise memory control, lower latency, or work in embedded environments without OS kernel support, Go’s GC becomes a burden.

item.title: MiBeeHive: The "Hive" Toolbox I Built for My Studio
item.description: Coming from an operations background, later transitioning to development, the number of projects I maintain keeps growing. Various middleware, databases, monitoring components… each version upgrade is a manual labor: go to the official site to find the download link, compare version numbers, manually download to the internal network, then distribute to each machine. I used to write a bunch of Shell scripts to periodically pull the latest versions to the LAN — functional but not user-friendly: scripts scattered everywhere, adding new software required writing parsing logic by hand, and there was nothing to check when things went wrong.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.5.0: Full ONVIF and Hardware Transcoding
item.description:
ONVIF cameras could be discovered and their stream URL retrieved — but that was just a corner of ONVIF: PTZ control, picture adjustment, and event subscription, the parts you actually use daily, were missing. And plenty of cameras output H.265 only, which browsers can’t play directly.

PTZ and picture, adjustable

  • Drive the camera with a joystick in the web UI — pan, zoom, one-tap home
  • Presets can be created, invoked, and deleted; frequent viewpoints are one tap away
  • Brightness, contrast, saturation, and sharpness adjust live on sliders, effective immediately
  • Events the camera reports (motion detection, alarms) show up in the web UI in real time

H.265 cameras play in the browser

  • Encoding is detected automatically; H.265 is transcoded to browser-playable H.264 on hardware when needed
  • Freeze-frame anti-flicker keeps the picture smooth through the transition
  • A new transcoding monitor page shows task status and performance at a glance

Steadier

  • The Xiaomi-camera disconnect churn is fixed: a full buffer drops the oldest frame instead of tearing down the whole session
  • Reconnects moved to tiered backoff with jitter — several cameras dropping at once no longer avalanche
  • A batch of fixes: first-boot Docker crash, false health alarms, a login-redirect loop

A protocol isn’t supported until all of it is.

item.title: Ownership and Borrowing: The Core of Rust Memory Safety
item.description:
This article is based on Rust 1.80+.

If you have a Go or Java background, the ownership system might be the most confusing concept in Rust. Go has a garbage collector (GC), and you rarely need to worry about when memory is freed. Rust takes a completely different approach—compile-time ownership rules guarantee memory safety, with zero runtime overhead.

The ownership system is the soul of Rust. It solves two classic problems: how to guarantee memory safety without using GC, and how to avoid data races. In other languages, these problems either require runtime checks or require extreme developer caution.

item.title: MiBeeSteward: Why I Built Another Device Management Tool in Go
item.description:
As a studio operator, the biggest pain point is never a specific problem — it’s the “not knowing” when devices multiply.

Not knowing which devices are alive, what services are running on them, whether a new machine has appeared on the network, whether a certain port is still open. This accumulated “not knowing” eventually becomes an outage.

My previous approach was a patchwork: Zabbix for monitoring, Nmap for scanning, Excel for asset tracking, Prometheus for metrics. Each tool is fine on its own, but together they’re a disaster — data silos, duplicate configuration, version drift, complex deployment.

item.title: Traits and Generics: Rust's Type Abstraction System
item.description:
In the previous articles, we explored Rust’s ownership system, error handling, and module management. Now we dive into the two core components of Rust’s type system—traits and generics. These form the foundation of Rust’s abstraction mechanisms: traits provide compile-time behavioral constraints, while generics bring type-safe parametric programming.

Rust’s trait system has similarities to Go’s interfaces, but the essence is different. Go’s interfaces use implicit implementation with duck typing, while Rust’s traits are explicitly declared contracts. More importantly, Rust’s traits combined with generics enable complete type checking and monomorphization at compile time, achieving zero-cost abstraction.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0: Timelapse and Transcoding
item.description:
Once recording is up and running, the disk cries first: one 1080p camera writes tens of GB a day, and 30-day retention eats most of a 1TB drive. The community reported the same thing over and over, and timelapse plus transcoding came up as the favored fixes.

Less disk

  • Timelapse: cameras whose scenes sit still most of the day need roughly 5% of the space for the same duration
  • Frames are skipped automatically while the picture stays static — idle time isn’t wasted
  • The extraction interval is configurable, and multiple cameras stagger themselves instead of spiking together

Recordings can be transcoded

  • H.264 ↔ H.265 in both directions, with historical recordings backfillable
  • Hardware encoding is auto-detected: use it when present (the Banana Pi M5 saturates H.265 hardware encoding), disable cleanly when not — the Raspberry Pi 3B is unaffected
  • Transcoding starts from the web UI, with status and progress visible

Steadier playback, easier diagnosis

  • A frozen picture is detected automatically
  • A class of H.265 playback corruption is fixed
  • Prometheus metrics and remote logging are wired in — problems get diagnosed from data instead of guesses

Keep the disk alive first.

item.title: Error Handling and Lifetimes: Result, Option, and Compile-Time Borrow Checking
item.description: If you’re used to Go’s if err != nil, encountering Rust’s error handling for the first time can be confusing. Go’s philosophy is explicit multi-return values, where errors are just ordinary values. Rust, on the other hand, elevates error handling to the type system level—a function that might fail must declare it explicitly in its return type. This design brings zero-cost abstractions but also introduces the two concepts that give beginners the most headaches: the Result<T, E> enum and lifetime annotations.

item.title: Standard Library, Concurrency, and async: Rust Chapter Finale
item.description:
After the journey of the first four articles—ownership and borrowing, type system, error handling, and pattern matching—we have now reached the Rust chapter finale, time to tie the scattered knowledge together.

This article focuses on Rust’s standard library concurrency tools and the async/await ecosystem. These are the most interesting comparative points between Rust and Go in the concurrency domain: Go makes concurrency look simple through goroutines and channels, while Rust makes concurrency safe and reliable through strict type systems and ownership constraints.

item.title: Building Nmap Fingerprint Loading Tools: Go vs Rust vs Zig Compared
item.description:
Nmap has the world’s most comprehensive network fingerprint database — over 6,000 service probe signatures and 5,000+ OS fingerprints. But its fingerprint engine is implemented in C++, tightly coupled to PCRE2 regex and nsock async I/O. Reusing it directly means accepting Nmap’s entire architectural constraints.

Building a custom fingerprint loading tool is valuable when you need to embed the fingerprint database into a standalone binary for offline scanning, integrate fingerprint matching into an automated pipeline, bypass Nmap’s licensing constraints for customized scan strategies, or use it as a foundational component in a security product.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.7.0: Timelapse v2 and the Hard-Fix Release
item.description:
After v0.6.0 shipped the timelapse pipeline, community feedback quickly listed the hard problems: an intermediate JPEG sequence ate too much space; H.265 cameras produced unplayable timelapse segments; dual-lens Xiaomi devices could only grab the main lens; and H.265 live view occasionally crashed outright.

Timelapse that actually works

  • Merging no longer goes through intermediate images: much smaller footprint, and the merged output is directly playable video
  • Timelapse segments from H.265 cameras play properly now
  • Merge windows come in selectable tiers (8 hours to 30 days) instead of a fixed daily run
  • Timelapse and regular recordings share one list — no flipping between two pages

Dual-lens Xiaomi, lens selectable

  • Dual-lens devices like the CW500 and Outdoor Cam 4 can target a specific lens
  • Chosen in the web UI, effective immediately

Steadier

  • The H.265 live-view crash is thoroughly fixed
  • The transcoding module was refactored into layers — adding new encoders or hardware no longer ripples through the whole pipeline

Fix what hurts first.

item.title: gortmplib vs go2rtc vs FFmpeg: RTMP Push Source Comparison & Integrating with Chinese Live-Streaming Platforms
item.description: To push camera feeds from the MiBee NVR project to a domestic live-streaming platform, there are three candidates: call FFmpeg directly, use the pure-Go gortmplib, or use go2rtc. All three “do RTMP”, but their behaviour against Chinese live-streaming platforms differs wildly — some disconnect instantly, some after a few seconds, some are rock solid. This post tears all three apart at the source level, and walks through the pitfalls and fixes for integrating with FMS-compatible domestic platforms.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.2.0: Distributed Discovery and Change Detection
item.description:
When v0.1.0 shipped, I wrote that it answers three questions: what devices are on the network, what they are, and how they relate. Honestly, v0.1.0 only answered the first half well — and only for the one LAN the center sat on.

The real-world layout is messier: one subnet in the office, one in the server room, another at home for test machines. The center lives in the office and literally cannot see the cameras in the server room. Getting it to scan the server room means crossing subnets — either opening up SNMP routing or just moving the center over there. Neither is elegant.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.9.0: Zero-Config Discovery, Debts Repaid
item.description:
As the camera count grows, so do the annoyances: adding an ONVIF camera meant typing IPs and opening a terminal; with 9 cameras starting together, the UI stalled for a dozen-plus seconds; every deployment began with checking whether FFmpeg was installed; and the older Xiaomi devices (Dafang, Xiaofang, Aqara G2) simply couldn’t be integrated.

Cameras that show up on their own

  • ONVIF cameras are discovered by the NVR the moment they power on; enter the password once in the web UI to activate — no IP fiddling
  • New and old devices live in one list
  • The TUTK-protocol legacy Xiaomi devices connect now too

It keeps up with many cameras

  • 9 cameras starting together no longer stall the UI (measured: 14.9 seconds down to milliseconds)
  • The storage layer was rewritten — recording writes no longer lock out queries
  • FFmpeg went from required to optional: it runs fine without it

A more complete interface

  • Missing translations and hardcoded Chinese strings fixed in one sweep
  • Recording-fragment cleanup, the Docker port clash, broken merge settings, and a batch of similar fixes

Debts get paid eventually.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.2.0 Internals: Anti-Entropy and Change Detection
item.description:
The previous post covered what v0.2.0 ships. This one covers why it’s designed that way — distributed consistency is the heaviest part of this release, and several seemingly casual decisions have specific trade-offs behind them.

The problem is clear: the center can only see its own LAN, but users have several. Dropping a center into every subnet isn’t realistic, so enter mibee-agent — a binary that only “scans local + reports to center.” But the moment an agent exists, it drags along a whole string of protocol questions: how to report, how to reconcile, how to detect offline, how not to overwhelm the center’s writes. Let’s take them one at a time.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.3.0: Topology, Certificates, and Containers
item.description:
Take over an unfamiliar LAN and the first thing you need is to figure out what’s on it — office, server room, and home subnets tangled together, no documentation left behind, a switch full of MACs nobody can name. MiBeeSteward exists for exactly that: scan the network and tell you what devices are there, what they are, and how they connect.

v0.3.0 goes after three specific pains left over from the last two releases:

Why Zig?

If you already know Go and Rust, you might ask: why look at a third systems language? Zig sits between the two, attempting to combine C’s lightness, Rust’s modern toolchain, and Go’s low barrier to entry.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.10.0: H.265 Live View and the Big Cleanup
item.description:
H.265 cameras used to be a half-broken experience: no live view on plain-HTTP LANs (HTTPS or nothing), merged recordings frequently black-screening on Edge, and timelapse merging not working at all.

H.265 plays everywhere now

  • H.265 live view works on plain-HTTP LANs — HTTPS no longer required
  • HTTPS environments use hardware acceleration automatically; everything else falls back to software decoding — both roads lead to playback
  • Recording merges, playback, and timelapse H.265 issues fixed in one pass

Better timelapse

  • Rewritten to v3: the 1-hour merge-window cap is gone
  • Merges are recorded in the database, progress queryable

A cleaner foundation

  • Login moved to signed tokens — no server-side session dependency, expiry under control
  • An architecture cleanup across config, DI root, and API routing, paving the way for stronger AI and more cameras

Clean the foundation before building higher.

item.description:

This article assumes you have Go or Rust experience and uses that as a reference frame to understand Zig’s design.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.11.0: fnOS Installs, GB/T 28181, and the Full-Day Timeline
item.description:
A few days after v0.10.0 went stable, fnOS users’ feedback boiled down to one sentence: it won’t install. Two older debts got settled in the same release: Hikvision/Dahua cameras couldn’t enroll — you either bought their NVR or stood up a separate GB platform; and playback showed one 30-second segment at a time, so reviewing a whole day meant clicking through segment by segment.

It installs now

  • All three install blockers are fixed: stalling on image downloads, a dead desktop icon, and a port field that rejected 9090 outright
  • The offline package bundles the full image set — works the moment it’s installed, no network needed
  • The online package is a few dozen KB and picks whichever of the China mirror or the official registry answers faster
  • The one-click install script auto-selects the same way
  • Synology, QNAP, and ZSpace store templates landed too

Easier to integrate

  • Hikvision/Dahua cameras enroll with a few filled-in fields — no vendor NVR, no separate platform (via the GB/T 28181 national standard)
  • Fully automatic after registration: a camera card per channel, recording starts on its own
  • PTZ, zoom, presets, and voice intercom work; the recordings on the camera’s own SD card are searchable and replayable
  • Hand Home Assistant-style integrations a dedicated key you can revoke on its own, without touching the global password
  • An IP change no longer breaks clients — they track the device, not the address

Playback that works

  • A whole day’s recordings stitch into one timeline — scrub to any moment
  • Segment switches no longer black-flash; the handover is invisible
  • Blank stretches from power cuts scrub right through without stalling
  • Authenticated live streams play on iPhone again

If it doesn’t install, it isn’t released.

item.title: The Rust and Go Ecosystems for ONVIF/GB28181: Library Selection, Source Reading, and a Hardware-Free Integration Path
item.description: The first three posts settled the protocol mechanics, the landscape, and the device side; the final question is concrete: which libraries to write it with. This survey went through everything usable in both ecosystems. The one-sentence verdict: ONVIF has workable libraries on both sides; the mature GB28181 implementations live on the Go/Java/C++ side while Rust’s are still young; and for streaming infrastructure (repackaging, distribution, egress) the Go ecosystem is clearly thicker.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.4.0: Discovery on the Router Itself
item.description:
Finding out what lives on your LAN used to mean active scanning — traffic, blind spots — or running in a container, which needed host networking just to see the full device table. Meanwhile the router knows everything already, and the discovery system was walking around it.

Live on the router, everything visible

  • The discovery program runs on the router itself: who joined the WiFi, who got which IP, who is online right now — the router already knows, so it just reads
  • No port scanning, no probe traffic; the full device list appears quietly
  • OpenWrt installs and runs as a first-class citizen

A more trustworthy device ledger

  • A device changing IP no longer forks into “old and new” phantom entries
  • One authoritative record per device; history stops diverging

The gateway already knows everything — just ask it.

item.title: Zig Memory Management: The Explicit Allocator Pattern
item.description:
This article is based on Zig 0.16.

In the previous articles we covered Zig’s basic syntax and error handling. Now we arrive at the most distinctive part of Zig—memory management.

If you come from Go or Rust, Zig’s memory philosophy will feel unfamiliar: it provides neither garbage collection nor an ownership system. Instead, it chooses a fundamentally different path—the Allocator Pattern. The core convention is remarkably simple, yet far-reaching:

Any function that might allocate memory must accept a std.mem.Allocator parameter.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.5.0: Three Things for the Enterprise
item.description: Bringing an internal-network device manager into a company — or any stricter environment — runs into three walls: SNMP stopped at v2c, with cleartext community strings riding the wire that no security audit passes and many hardened networks simply disable, paralyzing collection outright; permissions came in just two tiers, admin and user, so shared deployments couldn’t separate who operates from who merely looks; and the first question of a network postmortem — “when was this config changed, and by whom” — had no answer.

item.title: Taking Over onvif-go: Real-Camera Fixes, Zero Dependencies, and Service Facades
item.description:
MiBeeNvr talks to cameras over ONVIF, and this library is what sits underneath. ONVIF is the de facto standard for IP video surveillance equipment: device discovery, media profiles, PTZ control, event subscriptions — all one set of SOAP-over-HTTP service conventions. Any brand that claims ONVIF compliance can, in theory, be integrated through the same calls.

onvif-go is that stack implemented in Go. We did not write it from scratch: its upstream was 0x524a/onvif-go — the previous author reshaped it into its modern form of a client plus a virtual camera server (the git history still traces back to earlier Go ONVIF attempts in the community). But upstream stalled entering 2026: the last merged PR landed in mid-January, the v1.0-through-v1.1.3 release cadence from late 2025 never resumed, and three Improve Test Coverage issues filed in November 2025 sit unclaimed to this day. Meanwhile we hit two problems in our own camera pool that could only be fixed inside the library.

item.title: Four Protocol Libraries, Extracted: ONVIF and GB28181 in Go and Rust
item.description:
MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols. ONVIF is the de facto standard internationally — Hikvision, Axis, Dahua, and Bosch all speak it. GB/T 28181 is China’s national surveillance standard, unavoidable in government and state-owned projects. The device side (Raspberry Pi camera firmware, one Go and one Rust implementation) and the NVR side (MiBeeNvr, Go) both speak these two protocols, and the stacks have always lived inside the projects.

Two problems with that. First, this code is pickled in interop details — digest-auth qop handling, SIP Via-branch uniqueness, MANSCDP element-vs-attribute dual forms, TCP framing header byte counts — each one was ground out against a real platform, and a new project would have to grind them all again. Second, a library survey two weeks ago showed the open-source landscape for these protocols is unevenly populated; several positions have no one standing in them.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.12.0: Sub-streams, Adaptive Recording, and Full-path Observability
item.description:
MiBeeNvr v0.12.0 is out. This release goes after two everyday annoyances: watching the cameras on a phone, where a thumbnail-sized preview quietly pulls the full-resolution video underneath — eating data and heating the phone; and corridor or doorway cameras writing tens of GB a day that nobody ever replays.

Less disk

  • When nothing moves, the camera records less; the moment anything moves, it snaps back to full recording without dropping a frame. Quiet scenes measured at roughly 3/4 less disk
  • A louder sound, a doorbell, or a sensor signal also kicks it back to full recording
  • The replay timeline carries a green-to-red heat strip — the segments where something happened are visible at a glance
  • When the disk nears full, the quietest recordings are deleted first
  • Phone viewing defaults to a small, smooth stream: no stutter, no heat; one tap switches to HD for detail
  • When nobody is watching, that preview stream disconnects by itself — no camera connection or bandwidth tied up

item.description:
bpftrace is great for quick probing and ad-hoc debugging. For production-grade monitoring tools, you need full eBPF programs. The architecture splits into two layers:

  • User side: loader written in Go (or Rust / libbpf C), loading the eBPF program and reading events

item.title: From Compliance to Real-Time Defense: The Evolution of security-collector-exporter
item.description:
The Origin: Compliance Check Hassles

Anyone in operations knows there’s no escaping one hurdle for domestic servers: Cybersecurity Level Protection (GB/T 22239-2019, commonly known as “Level Protection 2.0”). Whether you’re Level 3 or Level 2, auditors come asking about these things:

  • Is SSH root login disabled? Are password policies compliant?
  • Is the firewall on? Is SELinux enforcing?
  • Are there expired accounts? What’s the password validity period?
  • Which ports are open? Are there high-risk services running?
  • Are audit logs enabled? How long are they retained?

There are plenty of compliance check tools on the market—search GitHub and you’ll find a bunch: Golin, EvaluationTools, Linux-Security-Compliance-Check, etc. But they all share one limitation: Run once, get a report, done. You check compliance today, and someone changes sshd_config tomorrow, turns off the firewall, installs a backdoor service—you’d never know.

item.title: security-collector-exporter v0.3.0: Real-Time Security Monitoring with eBPF
item.description:
From Static to Real-Time

The previous article introduced security-collector-exporter v0.1.0 — turning Linux security configuration states into Prometheus metrics. But v0.1.0 is essentially “snapshot-based”: periodically reading /etc, /proc, capturing the static configuration at a single point in time.

There’s an area of security operations that snapshots can’t cover: real-time security events. Someone running a reverse shell, a process escalating privileges, an abnormal network connection, someone loading a kernel module — these events happen and pass; you’d never see them at your next scrape.

item.title: security-collector-exporter: Monitoring Linux Security Auditing
item.description:
Why This Was Built

Anyone managing servers has probably had this experience: compliance audit comes, SSH into machines one by one to check—SSH config correct, SELinux enabled, firewall running, any expired accounts, password policies compliant. A few machines are fine; dozens or hundreds becomes purely manual grunt work.

And the more painful part: none of this has continuous monitoring. You check compliance today, someone changes a config tomorrow, and you’d never know.
